Why a single outlier makes the sample mean arbitrary

points.heading: The mean has zero breakdown
points.body: The sample mean is defined as the sum of observations divided by n. If any single observation gets arbitrarily large, the mean becomes arbitrarily large. Thus the breakdown point for the mean is 0.

points.heading: The median survives extremes
points.body: The median is the central value in a distribution where equal numbers of values lie above and below. If a minority of observations go to infinity, the median will not be arbitrarily bad. Its breakdown point is one half.

points.heading: When is the mean actually good?
points.body: Considering robustness and breakdown point, the mean works well only when the data contain zero outliers, no skewness, and unimodality. The median handles these deviations from normality much better.

posted.takeaway: Because a single outlier makes the sample mean arbitrary, consider nonparametric location tests for primary analysis.

posted.title: Linear or logistic regression? Look at your outcome

points.heading: The outcome dictates the model
points.body: Regression helps show how different factors connect to disease outcomes. The choice between linear and logistic regression hinges directly on how your dependent variable is measured.

points.heading: Linear models require continuous data
points.body: In linear regression, the dependent variable must be continuous, such as intraocular pressure or visual acuity. Independent variables may be continuous, binary, or categorical.

points.heading: Logistic models need binary outcomes
points.body: The distinguishing feature in logistic regression is that the dependent variable must be binary, meaning that the variable can only take two values, such as yes versus no.

points.heading: Comparing the effect metrics
points.body: Linear regression reports coefficients showing unit changes in the outcome. Logistic regression expresses predictor effects using an odds ratio to compare relative odds of the event.

posted.takeaway: Linear regression requires a continuous outcome, whereas logistic regression demands a binary dependent variable.

posted.title: Primary outcome: defined before, not after

points.heading: What the item asks
points.body: Report every prespecified primary and secondary outcome: measurement variable, analysis metric, method of aggregation and time point.

points.heading: Why it matters
points.body: Vague outcomes invite switching after the data are in, one of the best-documented sources of reporting bias.

points.heading: How to comply
points.body: Example: pain on a 0–10 numeric scale (variable), change from baseline (metric), mean (aggregation), at 12 weeks (time point).

posted.takeaway: An outcome is prespecified only if variable, metric, aggregation and time point are written first.

posted.title: Proxy and provider ratings differ from patient self-reports

points.heading: Who answers the questionnaire?
points.body: Assessments may be performed by rehabilitation providers, patients, or proxies, and their ratings can differ.

points.heading: Proxies overestimate disability
points.body: Proxy assessors tend to rate patients as more disabled than other functional measures suggest, and the gap grows with more impaired patients.

points.heading: The frame of reference trap
points.body: Healthcare professionals may tend to rate patients higher than patients rate themselves, possibly due to a difference in frame of reference.

posted.takeaway: Proxy and provider ratings can differ from patients' own, so use the same respondent type at every follow-up.

posted.title: How opaque reporting biases conclusions and prevents reliability judgment

points.heading: The danger of opaque reporting
points.body: Opaque reporting is directly associated with biased conclusions and, less directly, with errors in biomedical publishing and inefficient resource use.

points.heading: Readers cannot judge study reliability
points.body: Without knowing study details, readers cannot determine if results are trustworthy.

posted.takeaway: Without clear methodological details, readers cannot judge if study findings are reliable.

posted.title: Could a colleague rerun your literature search?

points.heading: What the item asks
points.body: Present the full search strategy for every database and register, including filters and limits, exactly as run.

points.heading: Why it matters
points.body: The search defines the evidence base. If it cannot be repeated, the review cannot be checked or updated.

points.heading: How to comply
points.body: Export each database's full query string into an appendix, with the date of the search and any language or date limits.

posted.takeaway: Report every search string, database, filter and date: reproducible or it is not systematic.

posted.title: Does watching a task before trying it in a virtual environment help restore hand function?

points.heading: The clinical question behind it
points.body: Researchers studied adults with hemiplegia to see if observing goal-directed daily actions before practicing them in virtual reality improves paretic hand dexterity.

posted.takeaway: Action observation combined with virtual reality appears to be more effective than virtual reality alone for promoting upper limb motor recovery.

posted.title: Why P-values do not belong in Table 1

points.heading: The real purpose of Table 1
points.body: Table 1 is for patient description, not hypothesis testing. Its real function is to summarize baseline characteristics so readers can gauge clinical comparability.

points.heading: The Table 1 fallacy in randomized trials
points.body: In randomized trials, a P-value tests whether treatment allocation occurred at random. Randomization guarantees this by definition, making significance testing of baseline balance completely illogical.

points.heading: Sample size distorts the results
points.body: P-values are sensitive to sample size. In huge cohorts, trivial differences produce significant P-values, while in small samples, true clinically meaningful imbalances remain hidden behind high P-values.

points.heading: Guidelines discourage them
points.body: Major guidelines like CONSORT for randomized trials and STROBE for observational studies advise against reporting P-values in baseline tables, urging researchers to…

posted.takeaway: Table 1 describes patients, not tests hypotheses. Drop P-values and use Standardized Mean Difference to assess clinical relevance.

posted.title: When the doctor becomes an investigator

points.heading: Dual roles in Clinical research
points.body: Balancing dual responsibilities can be difficult, and investigator enthusiasm may sometimes compromise ethical judgment.

points.heading: Benefit and risk balance
points.body: Benefit and risk are two faces of the same coin. The risk is assumed by participants while the benefit is reaped by a population.

points.heading: The Nuremberg Code (1947)
points.body: Formulated after WWII trials, the Nuremberg Code highlighted the need for informed consent, qualified scientists, and risk justification.

points.heading: Declaration of Helsinki
points.body: Developed by WMA in 1964, it binds the physician to ensure that the health of the patient will be the first consideration.

posted.takeaway: Doctor-researchers must prioritize patient welfare per the Declaration of Helsinki and Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines.

posted.title: Observational study? Name your biases in print

points.heading: What the item asks
points.body: Describe any efforts to address potential sources of bias: selection, information and confounding.

points.heading: Why it matters
points.body: Every observational design has bias. Readers judge your results by how openly you handled it, not by silence.

points.heading: How to comply
points.body: List your 3 most likely biases, then state the design or analysis step taken for each: restriction, matching, adjustment, sensitivity analysis.

posted.takeaway: State each likely source of bias and what you did about it: silence reads as blindness.

EU-HORIZON-BRIDGING-2027-06-02.summary: This call aims to bridge the gap between Horizon research outcomes and market deployment. Consortia of knowledge intermediaries—such as technology transfer offices, incubators, and innovation platforms—will scout Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe results and provide mentorship, training, and guidance. EU-HORIZON-HLTH-2027-01-CARE-02.summary: This call aims to reduce Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) resulting from polypharmacy (the use of three or more medications). Proposals should leverage pharmacogenomics, biomarkers, and digital technologies like AI and electronic health records to create personalized medicine strategies. Research should include clinical studies and address ethical, regulatory, and implementation challenges in healthcare systems.
